findings.title: The terminal privilege sweep bricks `npm run test:fund-user` on every fresh local chain, and the comment on the failing line still claims the deployer is an authorized minter
findings.severityRationale: C4 High requires assets stolen/lost/compromised — structurally impossible here (mock token, disposable chain, published key). C4 Medium requires protocol function or availability impact, or a value leak: a developer utility on chain 31337 is neither the protocol's function nor its availability, and no value moves. That lands it in QA/Low, and within that band it is a LOW rather than a bare QA note on two grounds: (i) it is a shipped, reproducible break of a command the project's own README instructs developers to run, introduced by the change under audit, so it has a real cost that recurs for every developer on every fresh chain; (ii) the in-source comment at the failing line now states the opposite of the truth, which converts a seconds-long fix into a misdirected debugging session — a comment that confidently asserts a false precondition is an aggravator within the band, not a neutral. Not raised further: the consumer sweep bounds the damage at exactly one dependent script.
findings.description: `_sweepResidualPrivileges` (DeployMocks.s.sol:1917) revokes the deployer's phUSD mint authority as the last transaction of every `npm run dev`. `script/interactions/FundTestUser.s.sol:46` calls `MockPhUSD(phUSD).mint(testUser, phUSDAmount)` inside a broadcast opened at :43 with `AddressLoader.getDefaultPrivateKey()` — anvil account #0, i.e. the deployer — and contains no `setMinter` re-grant anywhere in the file. Reproduced empirically on a fresh chain immediately after a clean `npm run dev`: `npm run test:fund-user` exits 1 with the verbatim revert `Not authorized to mint` (src/mocks/MockPhUSD.sol:48), trace tail `│   └─ ← [Revert] Not authorized to mint / └─ ← [Revert] Not authorized to mint / Error: script failed: Not authorized to mint`. The comment immediately above the failing call — `// Mint phUSD (deployer is authorized minter)` — is now false and will actively mislead whoever debugs this. An independent repo-wide consumer sweep confirms FundTestUser is the ONLY local consumer of the deployer's phUSD grant: simulate-yield.sh mints MockDola (permissionless), MintPhUSD.s.sol routes through PhusdStableMinter (own grant), FullFlowTest.s.sol uses minter.mint, and everything else targets permissionless mocks. However `script/interactions/README.md` points at `npm run test:fund-user` four times (:47, :283, :352, :383 — the last reading 'Fund test user first'), so the broken command sits inside the documented developer workflow rather than in an obscure corner. Story 079 found this, recorded it as Autonomous Decision 4 and Review Issue 1, and deliberately declined to fix it to honour its own single-file constraint; both of its validators endorsed that reading and both recommended scheduling the one-liner. Filing it here is that scheduling, not a disagreement.
findings.impact: A documented developer-onboarding command fails on every fresh local chain with a revert that points at the token rather than at the deploy script that removed the grant. No asset, availability or value impact — chain 31337 mock token, published key.
findings.recommendation: Add the one-line self-grant inside FundTestUser.s.sol, immediately after `vm.startBroadcast(deployerKey);` at :43 and before the mint at :46 — `MockPhUSD(phUSD).setMinter(deployer, true);` — since the deployer remains the token owner after the sweep. Update the now-false comment at :45 to say the script grants itself the right rather than assuming it. Prefer the self-grant over re-exempting the deployer in the sweep: the sweep's declarative end-state ACL is the more valuable artifact and should not be weakened to accommodate a utility script. Optionally symmetric: revoke again before `vm.stopBroadcast()` so the utility leaves the ACL as it found it.

Not Medium either, and this is the load-bearing judgement of the run: C4 Medium wants the protocol's function or availability impacted, or value leaked under stated assumptions. This finding impacts the coverage of a TEST, not the protocol. A rehearsal gap does not itself cause loss; it removes one gate that would have caught a loss caused by something else — and the something else that already got through is filed and acknowledged in its own right (85d794b3), where its severity properly lives. Counting the same escaped defect a second time here, on the rehearsal artifact, would double-book it and inflate the report. It is nonetheless a real Low rather than QA, on two independent grounds: the unmirrored index carries the highest-value movement in the whole cutover (a BPT custody transfer) and a different decimal class, so the gap is not a duplicate of the covered case; and the parameterised-LOOKING constant actively invites a false belief that re-targeting is cheap, which is a trap rather than a mere absence.
findings.description: DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol performs the swap on five indices — 1, 2, 3 (Uniboost, USDC 6dp), 4 (BalancerPoolerV2, USDS 18dp) and 7 (NudgeRatchet) — with pull/setDispatcher/setHook/replaceDispatcher call sites at :1300/:1341/:1342/:1363, :1456/:1519/:1520/:1528 and :1584/:1623/:1624/:1632. Phase 7.6 mirrors exactly one, on index 1. Indices 2 and 3 are genuine duplicates and cost nothing. Index 7's two distinguishing claims are honestly pinned by static assertions (hookTypeId, ratio == 100), both of which execute and pass. The change did not invent the residue; it converted a live retained balance on the LIVE dispatcher into a residue on an OFF-INDEX one. The replacement starts at zero retained prime (verified).
classification.whatAnOperatorGainsOrLoses: Nothing is gained by anyone. What an operator loses is knowledge of where the pot is: after the cutover the retained-prime pot silently splits across two addresses, and any pooling automation bound to the address-book dispatcher calls `pool()` on a contract whose retained balance is zero and reverts `Uniboost: nothing to pool` until fresh mints accrue, while the real balance sits on a retired contract nothing points at. Recoverable in one owner transaction once noticed.
attackPath: 1. Not an attack path — an operational-hazard path. No adversary is required or asserted.
2. `_rehearseDispatcherSwap` retires the incumbent Uniboost with a non-zero retained prime balance and no sweep or assertion.
3. The address book and every consumer repoint to the replacement, whose retained balance is zero.
4. Pooling automation targeting the address-book dispatcher reverts `Uniboost: nothing to pool`; the operator looks for the pot at the address the address book names and does not find it there.
5. Recovery: one owner `rescueERC20` on the retired contract — proved to work locally.
classification.likelihood: Certain on the local chain (measured). On mainnet the SHAPE is confirmed present — `_swapUniboost` (DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol:1443-1538) has no sweep either, and its indices 1/2/3 incumbents are live dispatchers accumulating real retained USDC from real user mints — but the MAGNITUDE is unmeasured and out of scope for this entry point.
classification.assumptions: That the retained-prime accounting behaves on mainnet as it does locally, and that the owner retains the `rescueERC20` capability and Uniboost ownership at cutover time.
classification.externalRequirements: For any mainnet consequence: a mainnet cutover must actually execute, and the incumbent must hold a non-trivial retained balance at that moment. Neither is established by this entry point.
